subject: mathematics
question_text: If f: A→B, g: B→C are two bijective functions then prove that (gof)⁻¹ = f⁻¹og⁻¹.

mark_split.label: Both sides have the same domain
Both sides give the same value

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.14 — LAQ chapter 1 Functions, question 2, on a ★★★ SSP. The 3+4 split is printed in that book's margin; appearance years are printed board-split as TS 16,20 and AP 16,17,19. Both are the publisher's claims until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms them. Re-cut to the 8-mark Section-C form of the 2026-27 pattern (TGBIE model paper w.e.f. 2026-27): the extra mark goes to Both sides give the same value.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove the reverse law for inverses — the two things you have to check, and how each one goes.

steps.label: Write what is given
steps.margin_note: No mark of its own. It fixes the two sides you are comparing, so the examiner can see you know what has to match.
lines: f: A→B and g: B→C are bijective functions.
Two functions are equal when they have the
same domain and the same value everywhere.

recall.must_convey: That proving two functions equal needs two things: the same domain, and the same value at every point. Naming only one is partial — confidence 0.5 or lower.
accept: to show two functions are equal check they have the same domain and the same value at every point
given f and g are bijections and we prove the inverse of gof equals f inverse composed with g inverse
first the domains must match then the values must match for every c
rendu functions equal avvalante domain same undali and value same undali
we compare domain first and then the value at each element

steps.why: Function equality is not obvious — two formulas can agree on values and still be different functions if their domains differ. Saying the test out loud is what makes the rest of the answer a proof.
common_mistakes: Jumping straight to the algebra without saying what equality of functions means.
Checking only the values and never the domain.

steps.label: Same domain
steps.margin_note: Three of the eight marks. Show that each side is a bijection from C to A. Write both lines — one for each side.

lines.text: Part 1 — the two sides have the same domain

lines: so (gof)⁻¹: C→A is also a bijection.
f⁻¹: B→A and g⁻¹: C→B are bijections,
so f⁻¹og⁻¹: C→A is also a bijection.
∴ (gof)⁻¹ and f⁻¹og⁻¹ both have domain C.

recall.must_convey: That gof is a bijection so (gof)⁻¹ goes C to A, and that f⁻¹ and g⁻¹ are bijections so f⁻¹og⁻¹ also goes C to A — therefore both sides share the domain C.
accept: gof is a bijection so its inverse goes from C to A and f inverse and g inverse compose to a map from C to A so both have domain C
both sides are bijections from C to A therefore the domains are the same
the inverse of gof is from C to A and f inverse g inverse is also from C to A same domain C
rendu sides C nunchi A ki velthai so domain same
check the arrows both sides start at C and end at A
reject: both are from C to A because they are inverses

steps.why: The inverse of a bijection is itself a bijection, and it runs backwards. Tracking which set each map starts from is what makes both sides land on C.
common_mistakes: Writing the composition in the wrong order, g⁻¹of⁻¹, which does not even have the right domain.
Asserting the domains match without showing each side is a bijection C→A.

steps.label: Same value
steps.margin_note: Five of the eight marks — the bigger half. Number your three facts (1), (2), (3) and quote the numbers when you use them. The examiner follows the numbers.

lines.text: Part 2 — the two sides give the same value

recall.must_convey: Take any c in C, unwind g⁻¹ to b and f⁻¹ to a, and separately note that (gof)⁻¹(c) is that same a — so both sides give a. The two chains must be tied together at the end.
accept: take c in C then g inverse of c is b and f inverse of b is a so f inverse g inverse of c is a and gof inverse of c is also a so they are equal
start from c work back to b then to a and show both sides give the same a
since f of a is b and g of b is c the inverse of gof sends c back to a and the composition of inverses also sends c to a
c teeskoni g inverse tho b vasthundi f inverse tho a vasthundi rendu sides a ne isthai
both sides evaluated at c give a therefore the functions are equal
reject: then I show the values are equal
it follows from the definition of inverse

steps.why: Applying f⁻¹og⁻¹ to c walks backwards along the same path that f then g walked forwards. That is why the composition of the inverses reverses the order.
common_mistakes: Applying f⁻¹ before g⁻¹ — the outer function g must be undone first.
Never stating 'for all c ∈ C', which is what turns two values into an equality of functions.
Using facts (1), (2), (3) without saying which line each step came from.

steps.label: Conclude
steps.margin_note: No separate mark, but the last line must be the thing the question asked for.
lines: Same domain and same value everywhere.

recall.must_convey: That both tests passed — same domain and same values — so the two functions are equal.
accept: same domain and same values so the inverse of gof equals f inverse composed with g inverse
both conditions hold therefore the two functions are equal
hence gof inverse equals f inverse g inverse
domain same value same so equal
we proved both parts so the result follows

steps.why: The question asked you to prove an equality of functions, so the final line should state that equality, not just the last calculation.
common_mistakes: Ending on the value calculation and never writing the equality.
